newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania president pledges help for pyramid victims.
newsitem.headline: Albania president pledges help for pyramid victims.

text.p: President Sali Berisha pledged on Tuesday to do his best to help impoverished Albanians who poured life savings into failed investment schemes, but said the government could not provide blank cheques or print money.

Hapless depositors, enticed by the pyramid schemes' promises of fast, high returns, waited for banks to offer the first partial refunds of trapped savings. Investors in one plan were to begin getting 60 percent of their stakes later in the day.

The ex-communist country's main opposition groups boycotted talks chaired by Berisha on dealing with the collapses. They renewed calls for the government to resign and demanded the release of people jailed after violent protests last month.
"The parties and trade unions agreed the government should not go beyond the state's real capabilities," Berisha, founder of the rightist Democratic Party, told reporters after the talks.
"They said the government must not adopt inflationary measures and must nMisfortune should not be cured with misfortune."

Berisha said the meeting had called for urgent help for ruined investors, by housing those who had sold apartments to plough money into the funds. But he rejected charges that his government was to blame by not warning uninitiated investors.

In Tirana's dusty streets, anxious depositors milled around curbside bank outlets where newspapers had instructed them to collect some of their lost savings. Many clutched ragged receipts and passbooks issued by the schemes.

"I will not ask for 60 percent of my savings. How do you expect me to be happy with that?" said a man in threadbare trousers. One elderly woman, close to tears, said she was left with barely enough money for a single meal a day.
Five schemes have collapsed, but compensation has been announced for only two whose assets were frozen in state banks.

Banks were to begin allocating 60 percent of deposits to investors in one "charity foundation" known as Populli. Refunds in a second scheme were to begin on Wednesday. Berisha said a third company popular in southern towns had all but collapsed and its assets would soon be turned over to depositors.
It was by no means certain new protests would erupt after a crackdown against demonstrators who set fire to public buildings last month to denounce the collapse of the schemes.

Opposition parties, united in a "Forum for Democracy" called for tighter parliamentary control over police and the courts and asked the United States and European Union "to use their influence to restore democracy in Albania".

"The Albanian people lived under a dictatorship for 40 years and it isn't so difficult to frighten them," Rexhep Mejdani, a leader of the main opposition Socialist party, told Reuters. "Intimidation is a problem, people are afraid."
Virtually every family in the country of 3.4 million committed funds to the schemes in the six years following the fall of eastern Europe's most repressive communist regime.

After last month's violent protests, nearly 150 people were arrested. Prosecutors are seeking long jail terms on rioting charges, prompting many would-be demonstrators to stay away from new rallies called last weekend.
Berisha said participants in his round table had demanded full implementation of the law to prevent fresh violence.
"The kingdom of crime will never come to Albania," he said.

His Democratic Party, first elected in 1992, backs market reforms and until last year boasted one of the best records for growth among ex-communist countries. It won a new term last year in polls criticised as unfair by Western observers.
